claims.text: An electroless-deposited ultrathin Ag coating can be applied to tungsten particles before W–Cu composite consolidation.
Coating the tungsten particles will produce a coherent, nanometer-thick Ag layer at the W/Cu interfaces.
A particle coating can form a modified interface with the surrounding metal matrix after consolidation.
The Ag layer provides an intermediate electronic structure between W and Cu.
The Ag interfacial layer reduces electron scattering across the W/Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial electron scattering lowers the thermal boundary resistance of the W–Cu composite.
Lower thermal boundary resistance increases the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
The Ag-coated W–Cu composite will have at least 20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The ductility of the Ag interfacial layer supports the mechanical integrity of the composite.
Interfacial particle coatings can improve bonding strength and mechanical properties in a consolidated metal-matrix composite.
The Ag-coated composite will retain mechanical properties comparable to or better than those of the uncoated W–Cu control.
The Ag layer resists irradiation-induced damage.
The Ag-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to or better than that of the uncoated W–Cu control.
Controlled-atmosphere sintering at 1000–1200 °C followed by annealing is suitable for producing the proposed Ag-modified W–Cu interface.
A post-sintering annealing step improves bonding at the proposed Ag/W/Cu interfaces.
The predicted benefits will persist at approximately 500 °C under representative neutron and ion irradiation associated with fusion-reactor joints.
The benefits depend on maintaining the Ag coating at an optimal thickness.
An excessively thick or discontinuous Ag layer may create brittle interfaces or processing defects that compromise durability or irradiation performance.
